description: Redirect chains whose hostile hop is not the first one. urls.json's redirect rows all turn bad immediately, which tests that hop 1 is checked and says nothing about hop 3 — and a guard that validates the URL it was given and then follows Location headers with the platform's redirect handling passes every one of those rows while being completely open.
notes: `hops` is the response served for each request in order. A hop with a `location` is a redirect; the final hop is the real response. Hostnames resolve as declared in `resolver`, which is merged over the default table in test/net-stubs.ts.
`connects` is how many requests the connector should have seen when the chain ends. It is the assertion that matters: the refusal must happen BEFORE the hostile hop is requested, not after.

worker/lib/guard.ts caps the chain at GUARD_LIMITS.maxRedirects (3) and re-validates each hop from scratch — userinfo, scheme, literal address, then resolution — so every property urls.json checks on hop 0 is checked again on every hop.

cases.note: Three entirely ordinary public hops, then the private one. Every hop before it was fetched — which is correct and is exactly why the check has to run on all of them rather than on the URL the caller supplied.

The last hop is the metadata service written in hex. Both defences have to hold at once on a redirect target: the alternate-encoding parse AND the per-hop re-validation. Also a 307 rather than a 302, because a guard that only recognises 301/302 stops following at the interesting moment and reports success.
The last hop is a perfectly ordinary NAME that happens to resolve into RFC1918. The literal check on the Location header does not catch this; only re-resolving the new host does.

Rebinding and redirection composed. The double lookup has to happen on every hop, not only on the URL the caller handed us — a guard that resolves twice for hop 0 and once per hop afterwards is open here.
Credentials introduced by the SERVER rather than by the caller. The URL we were given was clean; the one we were told to go to is not, and it is re-validated from scratch.
A downgrade to a genuinely public host. Still refused: an http hop is a channel we can make no statement about, and the report says things about TLS.
A scheme-relative Location. It inherits https from the current URL, so it is not a downgrade — it is a host change that a check looking for `http://` in the header would not see at all.
An ordinary relative redirect, resolved against the current URL and staying on the same public host. It must go through: over-blocking redirects would break a large share of real endpoints.
Three redirects is the documented maximum and must be allowed. The boundary is tested from both sides because an off-by-one here is either a broken product or a longer chain than the policy promises.

The fourth redirect is refused. Note the chain is not a loop — a hop limit that only catches self-referential loops does not bound a chain of distinct URLs, and it is the count that costs us, not the repetition.

The response caps are not bypassed by arriving via a redirect. Worth a row because the caps are applied to the terminal response, and the terminal response is the one whose URL nobody validated by hand.
